---
title: "Build a local development workflow you can reset in minutes"
date: 2026-04-12
categories: ["development"]
tags: ["local-dev", "docker", "direnv", "makefile"]
summary: "Set up a repeatable local development workflow with one entrypoint, repo-owned defaults, and fast verification."
slug: "local-development-workflow"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to build a repeatable local development workflow with [Git](https://git-scm.com/), [Docker Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/), [direnv](https://direnv.net/), and [GNU Make](https://www.gnu.org/software/make/) so you can clone a project, start it fast, and recover from drift without guesswork.

## Prerequisites

- A project tracked in Git
- Docker and Docker Compose installed
- `direnv` installed and hooked into your shell
- `make` available in your terminal

## Start With One Command

Your workflow needs one obvious entrypoint. If a new shell session makes you remember five commands, your setup is already drifting.

```make
APP_NAME := app

.PHONY: setup up down logs test reset

setup:
	cp -n .env.example .env || true
	direnv allow
	docker compose pull
	docker compose up -d

up:
	docker compose up -d

down:
	docker compose down

logs:
	docker compose logs -f $(APP_NAME)

test:
	docker compose exec $(APP_NAME) php artisan test

reset:
	docker compose down -v
	docker compose up -d --build
```

This gives you one place to start: `make setup`. It also turns the common tasks into short, memorable commands, which matters once you start cleaning up config.

## Keep Environment Defaults In The Repo

A local workflow breaks when setup lives in memory instead of files. Put the safe defaults in the repository so every clone starts from the same baseline.

```bash
# .envrc
export COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=myapp
export APP_PORT=8080
export DB_PORT=3307
export APP_ENV=local
```

```dotenv
# .env.example
APP_NAME="My App"
APP_ENV=local
APP_DEBUG=true
APP_URL=http://localhost:8080
DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=db
DB_PORT=3306
DB_DATABASE=app
DB_USERNAME=app
DB_PASSWORD=secret
```

The `.envrc` file loads shell-level defaults every time you enter the repo. The `.env.example` file gives your app a known starting point, but you still need services that match those values.

## Run Services In Containers, Keep Editing Local Files

You want the app runtime to be predictable, but you also want your editor, shell history, and git tools to stay fast. Containers are a good fit for services and runtimes because they remove machine-specific drift.

```yaml
services:
  app:
    image: php:8.3-cli
    working_dir: /var/www/html
    volumes:
      - ./:/var/www/html
    command: php -S 0.0.0.0:8080 -t public
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: mysql:8.0
    environment:
      MYSQL_DATABASE: app
      MYSQL_USER: app
      MYSQL_PASSWORD: secret
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: root
    ports:
      - "3307:3306"
    volumes:
      - db_data:/var/lib/mysql

volumes:
  db_data:
```

This setup keeps your code on the host and mounts it into the container, so file edits show up immediately. The database also gets a named volume, which is convenient for day-to-day work, but it creates one more thing you need to reset on purpose.

## See The Workflow Before You Add More Tools

Once you have shell config, app config, and containers, the workflow stops being a list of commands and becomes a system.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Clone repo] --> B[Enter project directory]
    B --> C[direnv loads .envrc]
    C --> D[make setup]
    D --> E[docker compose starts services]
    E --> F[App reads .env]
    F --> G[You develop and run tests]
    G --> H[make reset when state drifts]
```

This is the loop you want to protect. If you add another tool, make it fit this flow instead of creating a second setup path.

## Verify The Workflow On A Fresh Shell

A workflow is only real if it works from a clean starting point. Test it the same way a teammate or future-you would hit it.

```bash
git clone <your-repo-url>
cd <your-repo-directory>
direnv allow
make setup
curl -I http://localhost:8080
make test
```

These commands verify the full path from clone to running app. If one of them fails, fix the workflow files before you write more documentation, because the broken step is the real draft.

{{< callout type="tip" >}}
When a local stack starts behaving strangely, run `make reset` before you start debugging application code. You need a clean runtime before you can trust the symptoms.
{{< /callout >}}

## Keep Local Development Boring

The best local workflow is easy to forget because it keeps doing the same thing every time. One command starts it. Repo-owned defaults define it. A clean reset restores it.

That simplicity is what lets you add better automation later, but only after the base path is solid.

---
title: "Migrate a small Node toolchain to pnpm"
date: 2026-04-12
categories: ["tooling"]
tags: ["nodejs", "pnpm", "migration"]
summary: "Learn how to move a small Node project from npm to pnpm so your installs stay fast and predictable."
slug: "migrate-node-toolchain-to-pnpm"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

If your [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) project still leans on [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/) by habit, this section shows you how to move to [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) so your installs stay faster, stricter, and easier to trust.

## Prerequisites

- A working Node.js project with a `package.json`
- `pnpm` installed on your machine
- A clean git working tree

## Replace npm lockfiles and install with pnpm

Start by removing the old lockfile, then let pnpm build a fresh one from the dependencies you already declared.

```bash
rm -f package-lock.json
pnpm install
```

This drops the npm lockfile and creates `pnpm-lock.yaml`. You now have one package manager in charge, which matters before you touch scripts or CI.

If your project exposes package-manager intent, pin it there too.

```json
{
  "packageManager": "pnpm@10.0.0",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "build": "vite build",
    "test": "vitest run"
  }
}
```

This tells other developers, and your automation, which tool should drive installs. It also keeps the migration visible in the one file every contributor already checks.

## Update automation to use the same command

A migration only sticks when your local shell, CI job, and docs all call the same tool.

```yaml
steps:
  - name: Install dependencies
    run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

  - name: Run tests
    run: pnpm test
```

This keeps CI aligned with your new lockfile. If automation still runs `npm install`, you have not finished the migration yet, so verification is next.

## Verify the new toolchain

Run the same commands a new contributor or CI runner would use.

```bash
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm build
pnpm test
```

These commands confirm the lockfile is usable, the app still builds, and your test entrypoint still resolves. Once that passes, you can clean up old setup notes and stop carrying both workflows.

---
title: "Build a repeatable workflow you can trust"
date: 2026-04-12
categories: ["workflow"]
tags: ["workflow", "process", "writing"]
summary: "Learn a simple workflow you can repeat without rebuilding the process every time."
slug: "build-a-repeatable-workflow-you-can-trust"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to build a repeatable workflow so you can start clean, move in order, and verify the result before you stop.

## Prerequisites

- A task you do more than once
- A place to write the steps down
- A clear result you can check at the end

## Turn the Work Into Fixed Stages

A repeatable workflow starts when you stop treating the job like a fresh puzzle.

Break it into stages. Keep them stable. Give each stage one purpose.

You can use four:

{{< steps >}}
{{< step "Prepare" >}}
Gather the files, notes, or inputs you need before you start. This keeps you from bouncing around later.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Do the work" >}}
Make the change, write the draft, or run the task. Stay inside the scope you set in the first stage.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Check the result" >}}
Compare the outcome to your expected result. If you cannot tell whether it worked, the workflow is still incomplete.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Record what changed" >}}
Write down what mattered: the final output, any fixes, and anything you should remember next time.
{{< /step >}}
{{< /steps >}}

Those stages give your work a shape. But a shape alone is not enough. You still need a trigger that tells you what to do first.

## Start With the Same First Move Every Time

Pick one action that always begins the workflow.

Make it small. Make it obvious.

Open the task. Read the goal. Write the expected outcome in one sentence.

That sentence keeps you from drifting. It also gives you something concrete to test at the end.

If the first move changes every time, the workflow stays fragile. The next part fixes that.

## Write the Steps So You Can Follow Them Cold

Write the workflow as if you will use it on a tired day.

Use direct instructions. One action per line. Cut anything that sounds clever but does not help you act.

Good workflow notes sound like this:

- Define the result.
- Gather the needed inputs.
- Do the task.
- Verify the output.
- Record the final state.

That list is short on purpose. You should be able to scan it and move. But speed is not the goal here. Consistency is.

## Verify the Workflow Before You Trust It

Run the workflow from the top without filling in missing steps from memory.

Pay attention to hesitation. If you stop and wonder what comes next, the workflow needs one more sentence.

You are not testing whether you can improvise. You are testing whether the process can carry you.

Once it survives that check, you have something you can reuse, teach, and improve. That is enough for today.

## Turn Vague Process Notes Into Concrete Steps

If your source notes say things like "momentum," "seamless," "robust," or "transformative," stop and name the work.

Your reader cannot act on mood words. Your reader can act on steps, checks, and decisions. That is the difference between a post that sounds polished and a post that teaches.

{{< compare >}}
{{< before >}}
The new workflow creates momentum across the team and gives you a seamless handoff between planning and delivery. The result is a more robust process that feels transformative in day-to-day work.
{{< /before >}}
{{< after >}}
The workflow starts with a written plan in the repo. You turn each step into a small task, assign an owner, and verify the result before merge. That cuts handoff mistakes because the next person can see the exact state of the work.
{{< /after >}}
{{< /compare >}}

The second version gives your reader something to copy. But you still need to show what that process looks like in practice.

```markdown
1. Write the plan in `docs/plan.md`.
2. Split the work into tasks that each change one part of the system.
3. Link every task to a file, command, or test.
4. Run the checks before review.
5. Record follow-up work instead of hiding it in prose.
```

This turns a fuzzy "better workflow" claim into a repeatable process. Your reader can now see where the work starts, how it moves, and what counts as done.

When you revise your draft, replace every abstract benefit with one visible behavior. That is what makes the next section worth reading.

# Saving Private Ryan (1998): ★★★½

*Directed by Steven Spielberg. Starring Tom Hanks, Tom Sizemore, Edward Burns, Barry Pepper. 169 min.*

---

*Saving Private Ryan* earns its reputation honestly, even if the reputation has flattened the movie into a synonym for "realistic war film." What Spielberg is trying to do is clear from the first twenty minutes: throw you into combat with enough chaos, noise, and confusion that the usual movie-war glamour burns off immediately. He mostly succeeds. The film is at its best when it remembers that battle is not just spectacle. It is disorientation, bad information, and a chain of exhausted men making decisions they barely have time to understand.

The Omaha Beach landing is still the benchmark because it is built around clarity inside confusion. You never mistake the terror for visual mush. The ramps drop, men are cut down before they can orient themselves, and Hanks' Captain Miller moves through the killing field in a daze that feels frighteningly physical. Spielberg and Janusz Kaminski give you blown-out flashes, muffled sound, and brief tactical snapshots: the Bangalore torpedoes, the machine-gun nests, the medics working on men who are already gone. The sequence is brutal, but it is not empty brutality. You understand what the soldiers are trying to do, how badly it is going, and what it costs to gain a few yards of shingle.

What makes the film more than a technical exercise is the stretch that follows. The mission itself is contrived in a way that has always bothered people, and fairly so. The movie asks you to accept a sentimental premise so it can study the men ordered to carry it out. That trade mostly works because the squad feels specific. Barry Pepper's Jackson praying before a shot, Giovanni Ribisi's Wade breaking down for his mother, Adam Goldberg and Edward Burns snapping at each other like men running on fumes instead of heroism, all of that gives the film texture. The quiet scene where Miller finally tells the others about his life back home lands because the movie has earned a little stillness.

It is also a film with a definite perspective on war, and the perspective is harsher than its reputation suggests. This is not a celebration of combat skill for its own sake. The final bridge battle is exciting, but it is also desperate, improvised, and full of ugly deaths. When Upham freezes on the stairs while Mellish is killed upstairs, Spielberg forces the point harder than some viewers like, but it works. Cowardice, paralysis, and moral failure belong to war too. So do useless deaths. So does the feeling that even victory arrives covered in waste.

The film is less steady in its middle act. A few speeches push too hard for nobility, and the framing device with the older Ryan has always felt more insistent than moving. Still, the craftsmanship is overwhelming, the period detail is convincing without showing off, and the combat remains legible in a way too many modern war films still fail to manage. It also sends you back to the history, which is one of the best compliments you can pay a movie like this.

This is easy to recommend to almost anyone interested in war films, though it is not casual viewing and never should be. I would not call it perfect. I would call it essential.

★★★½

---
title: "Turning a Coding Session Into a Blog Draft"
date: 2026-04-12
categories: [ai]
tags: [claude-code, writing, workflow]
summary: "How I turned a useful coding session into a structured draft without flattening the real decisions that made it worth reading."
slug: "turning-a-coding-session-into-a-blog-draft"
draft: true
---

A lot of coding sessions feel interesting while they are happening and completely flat an hour later. The problem is not that the work was trivial. The problem is that the useful part usually lives in the tension: the false starts, the boundary decisions, the one small constraint that forced a better shape. If I wait too long, I remember the outcome and forget the reasoning.

That came up again while shaping a workflow for turning development sessions into blog posts. I did not want another generic "here is what I built" write-up. I wanted a draft that preserved the actual arc of the work: what was hard, what I tried, what finally clicked, and what another developer could reuse.

## The Problem / Context

The raw material from a coding session is messy. It has shell commands, partial ideas, code diffs, and little course corrections that matter a lot in the moment. A blog post needs shape. If I summarize too aggressively, I lose the parts that make the post useful. If I keep too much chronology, I end up with a transcript nobody wants to read.

I have seen this go wrong both ways.

One failure mode is the polished recap that skips the real work. It reads cleanly, but it teaches almost nothing because the interesting decisions are gone. The other failure mode is dumping every step in order. That keeps the facts, but it forces the reader to sort signal from noise.

The session-to-blog workflow needed a middle path. The draft had to feel like a build log written by someone who was actually there, not a cleaned-up tutorial pretending the solution was obvious from the start.

## What I Tried / The Approach

The first useful decision was to stop treating the session like a timeline and start treating it like an arc.

I broke the draft around four sections:

```markdown
## The Problem / Context
## What I Tried / The Approach
## The Solution
## What I Learned
```

That sounds simple, but it fixed a real problem. A coding session is full of motion, but readers do not need every motion. They need the motions that changed the result.

I also wanted the draft to be publishable in the blog without extra cleanup, so I pinned down the Hugo shape up front:

```yaml
---
title: "Turning a Coding Session Into a Blog Draft"
date: 2026-04-12
categories: [ai]
tags: [claude-code, writing, workflow]
summary: "How I turned a useful coding session into a structured draft without flattening the real decisions that made it worth reading."
slug: "turning-a-coding-session-into-a-blog-draft"
draft: true
---
```

That removed one whole class of friction. If the draft is going into `content/posts/<category>/<slug>/index.md`, I should produce it that way from the start.

My first instinct was to make the draft generator focus on completeness. Pull in all the details, mention every notable command, preserve the sequence. That was the wrong emphasis. Completeness is easy. Judgment is harder.

The better filter was this:

- Is there a clear problem-to-solution arc?
- Did the session produce a reusable lesson?
- Would another developer learn more from the failed attempt than from the final code alone?

Once I used those questions, the writing got sharper.

For example, this is the kind of command-level detail that belongs in a draft when it supports the story:

```bash
ls /home/jones/dev/blog/content/posts/*/
grep -rl "workflow" /home/jones/dev/blog/content/posts/
```

That does two things. It checks whether I am about to repeat myself, and it forces me to ask whether the angle is actually new. A lot of technical blogs quietly rot because they keep publishing the same post with slightly different nouns.

The other important part was tone. I wanted first person, conversational, and technical. Not hype. Not a tutorial voice pretending I had the answer from line one. That meant writing sentences like a working engineer writes after a real session: direct, specific, and a little opinionated where it helps.

## The Solution

The solution was to build the draft around decisions, not chronology.

I treated the session as source material and extracted only four kinds of facts:

- The real problem that created pressure.
- The wrong turn or incomplete first attempt.
- The final working approach.
- The lesson that would survive outside this exact project.

That gave me a repeatable structure for the post without forcing every post to sound the same.

Here is the core shape I ended up using:

```markdown
## The Problem / Context
Set the scene in a few sentences. Name the tension early.

## What I Tried / The Approach
Show the work. Keep the failed attempt if it teaches something.

## The Solution
Give the final pattern, code, or workflow in concrete terms.

## What I Learned
End with the durable lesson and any caveats.
```

What changed the quality of the draft was being stricter about what counted as concrete. "I improved the workflow" is useless. "I moved from a chronological recap to a problem-solution structure because the transcript buried the key decisions" is useful.

The same rule applied to examples. If I include code or commands, they have to earn their place. A short YAML front matter block is useful because it shows how the draft lands in Hugo. A section outline is useful because it explains the shape of the writing. A random shell history dump is just noise.

I also kept `draft: true` in the front matter by default. That matters more than it sounds. It turns the writing process into a review step instead of a publishing step. I can get the thinking onto the page while it is still fresh, then come back and tighten the title, trim repetition, and remove anything that only made sense inside the session.

The end result was not a transcript, and it was not a generic summary. It was a draft with enough structure to read cleanly and enough session detail to feel honest.

## What I Learned

The useful part of a coding-session post is rarely the final code by itself. It is the moment where a vague mess became a deliberate approach.

That changed how I think about this kind of writing. I do not need to preserve everything. I need to preserve the decisions that carried the work forward.

I also learned that a draft gets better when the constraints are explicit. Hugo front matter. Category. Slug. Draft flag. Four sections. Those constraints sound mechanical, but they free up attention for the part that actually matters: saying what happened in a way another developer can use.

If I keep using this workflow, I will probably get stricter about overlap checking. It is easy to convince yourself a post is new because the session felt new. That is not the same thing. The angle has to be fresh too.

The main takeaway is simple: write around the tension, the attempt, the fix, and the lesson. That is usually enough. When a session has something worth sharing, those four pieces carry most of the weight.

Ahnii!

I spent a recent build session tightening the shape of my work instead of adding one more loose feature. I was moving between [Waaseyaa](https://waaseyaa.org), [Minoo](https://minoo.live), and [OIATC](https://oiatc.waaseyaa.org), and the real task was not just shipping code. It was making sure the pieces still belonged to the same vision.

## The Problem / The Why

I have been thinking a lot about what it means to build infrastructure from where I stand, not from where the market tells me I should stand. That sounds abstract until I am deep in a session and looking at three or four systems that all want attention at once. One needs a cleaner interface. One needs better internal rules. One needs language that actually says what it is for. The pressure is always to move faster, add more, announce more.

What I am trying to protect is coherence.

A lot of software ends up fragmented because the work gets pulled apart by convenience. One tool for publishing. Another for community. Another for operations. Another for AI. Before long the whole thing becomes a stack of dependencies and borrowed assumptions. I am trying to do something harder than that. I am trying to build systems that can hold Indigenous governance, language, memory, and local ownership without forcing all of it through somebody elses frame first.

That is why this session mattered. I was not chasing a flashy milestone. I was checking whether the foundation still matched the reason I started.

## What You Built / What You Found

The main thing I worked on was alignment between the framework level and the product level. In practice, that meant looking at where Waaseyaa is supposed to stay general and where Minoo is allowed to become specific. I do not want the framework turning into an accidental product, and I do not want the product carrying framework decisions that should stay reusable.

That sounds like a small distinction, but it changes how I write almost everything.

In this session I tightened naming, pulled apart a few responsibilities that had started to blur together, and kept asking the same question: is this part of the engine, or is this part of the community it is meant to serve? I found a few places where I had let momentum make the decision for me. That is usually how drift starts. Not with one bad choice, but with five convenient ones.

I also spent time looking at OIATC as more than a side project. I keep coming back to the fact that education, platform work, and digital sovereignty are not separate tracks for me. They are one body of work. If I am building tools but not building the conditions for people to understand and govern those tools, I am only doing half the job. That realization keeps pushing me away from feature thinking and back toward institution thinking.

What I found in the session was simple. The work gets stronger when I slow down enough to name what each piece is actually for. I do not need every system to do everything. I need each one to be clear, durable, and able to grow without losing its purpose.

There is also a personal side to this. Some sessions feel productive because I can point to a long list of finished tasks. This one felt productive because the architecture got quieter. Fewer mixed signals. Less internal contradiction. More confidence that I am not building myself into a corner.

## Where It's Going

The next step is not a big reveal. I need to keep shaping the boundaries between the framework, the platform, and the educational work so each can move faster without dissolving into the others. There is still a lot to prove. I need stronger defaults, better writing around the intent of each project, and more discipline about what belongs now versus later.

I also want to keep writing from inside these build sessions, because that is where the real story is. Not the polished launch version. The part where the ideas meet resistance, where the scope gets cut down, where the structure finally starts making sense.

I am building for durability. I am building for Indigenous ownership on the web. I am building systems that I hope can carry more than my own use case. That takes longer. It should take longer.

I am going to keep writing as this takes shape. Subscribe to follow the build, or reply if there is a part of this work I should stay with longer.

# Configure Your Application

This section shows you how to define configuration defaults, override them per environment, and verify the final values your application loads.

## Define Your Base Configuration

Start with a single file that holds the values you expect in every environment. Keep it boring. Defaults should be safe, readable, and easy to override later.

```yaml
app:
  name: Acorn
  env: production
  debug: false
  url: https://example.com

database:
  host: 127.0.0.1
  port: 5432
  name: acorn
  user: acorn
  password: null
```

This [`YAML`](https://yaml.org/) file gives you a stable baseline. You can commit it to your repo because it contains structure, not secrets.

## Override Values With Environment Variables

Use environment variables for anything that changes between machines. Secrets go here too. That keeps your base config clean and keeps credentials out of version control.

```bash
APP_ENV=local
APP_DEBUG=true
APP_URL=http://localhost:3000
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=acorn_dev
DB_USER=acorn
DB_PASSWORD=secret
```

These values usually live in a `.env` file during local development. In production, you set the same keys through your process manager, container platform, or host.

## Map Environment Variables Into Config Values

Your application still needs one place where raw environment variables become typed configuration. Do that mapping explicitly. You avoid surprises later.

```php
return [
    'app' => [
        'name' => env('APP_NAME', 'Acorn'),
        'env' => env('APP_ENV', 'production'),
        'debug' => filter_var(env('APP_DEBUG', false), FILTER_VALIDATE_BOOL),
        'url' => env('APP_URL', 'https://example.com'),
    ],
    'database' => [
        'host' => env('DB_HOST', '127.0.0.1'),
        'port' => (int) env('DB_PORT', 5432),
        'name' => env('DB_NAME', 'acorn'),
        'user' => env('DB_USER', 'acorn'),
        'password' => env('DB_PASSWORD'),
    ],
];
```

This file turns string input into values your code can trust. Notice the cast on `DB_PORT` and the boolean filter on `APP_DEBUG`. Those small choices prevent messy bugs.

## Load Configuration in the Right Order

Order matters. Load defaults first. Apply environment overrides second. Cache the merged result only after both layers are in place.

```bash
php artisan config:clear
php artisan config:cache
```

The first command removes stale cached values. The second rebuilds the cache from your current files and environment, so the application boots with the right settings.

## Verify the Final Configuration

Do not assume the override worked because the file looks correct. Read the resolved value from the running app.

```php
var_dump(config('app.env'));
var_dump(config('app.debug'));
var_dump(config('database.host'));
```

This gives you the actual values after defaults, environment variables, and casting have all been applied. If something looks wrong here, the problem is in your load order or your variable names, not in the feature that reads the config.

## Keep Secrets Out of Base Config

Store API keys, database passwords, and private tokens in environment variables only. Leave placeholders or `null` in committed files.

```yaml
auth:
  github_client_id: null
  github_client_secret: null
```

This makes the expected shape of the config obvious without exposing credentials. New developers can see what must be supplied before the app can boot cleanly.

## Name Configuration Keys for Real Use

Choose names that match how you read them in code. Short names help, but clarity matters more.

Use `database.host`, not `dbStuff.serverValue`. Use `app.debug`, not `enableMagicMode`. When a key name is plain, the rest of the workflow stays plain too.

# Package Overview

This package gives you a clear way to add the feature to your application without extra framework glue.

## Install the Package

Add the package with Composer, then let your application discover it.

```bash
composer require vendor/package
```

This installs the package and updates your `composer.json` file. If your framework supports package discovery, the package is available after install.

## Configure the Package

Publish the config file if you need to change defaults.

```bash
php artisan vendor:publish --tag=package-config
```

This copies the package config into your application so you can edit it directly. If the defaults already fit your setup, you can skip this step.

## Use the Main Service

Call the package through its main service class.

```php
use Vendor\Package\PackageManager;

$manager = app(PackageManager::class);
$result = $manager->run([
    'source' => 'input.json',
    'mode' => 'strict',
]);
```

This resolves the service from the container and runs the package with your input. The returned value contains the processed result for the current request.

## Understand What the Package Handles

You pass in structured input.

The package validates that input, applies its rules, and returns a consistent output shape.

You do not need to wire up the internal services yourself. The package registers what it needs through its service provider.

## Extend the Package

Swap the default behavior when your application needs custom rules.

```php
use Vendor\Package\Contracts\RuleEngine;
use App\Packages\CustomRuleEngine;

$this->app->bind(RuleEngine::class, CustomRuleEngine::class);
```

This replaces the default rule engine with your own implementation. Use this when the built-in behavior does not match your domain rules.

## Check When to Use It

Use this package when you need one place to handle the feature across multiple parts of your application.

Skip it if you only need a small one-off helper. The package is most useful when the same logic shows up in more than one workflow.
